![Research](cid:image_dccc2f76-b125-11f1-b79c-85eb549cca22_1_2)

| | | | | ![](cid:image_dccc2f76-b125-11f1-b79c-85eb549cca22_1_3)  
---  
Global Credit Strategy & Securitized Products Research  
**The State of AI Financing: A Pause, Not a Pullback**  
| | | [**Read Full Report**](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/dccc2f76-b125-11f1-b79c-85eb549cca22?t=1790953505:9363:2233496:816774ccf5ea&m=1&ch=Outlook Blastmail#e=ZmVsaXBlLm1vbnRlaXJvQGNhcHN0b25lLmNvbS5icg==)  
---  
  


(PDF: 42 Pages)  
---  
  


| | **Global**  
---  
Fernanda Lima, Carolyn L Campbell, Vishwanath Tirupattur, Vishwas Patkar,
James Egan, Aron Becker & 12 more...  
_October 1, 2026_  
  
---  
  


| | | September marked the second-lowest month of AI-related supply this year, with only ~$23bn globally. In our view, this slowdown is temporary and driven by a combination of significant front-loading of issuance in the year and building political/regulatory constraints. We expect a busier fall and 4Q, as the focus shifts to 2027 capex.   
---  
  


| | **Key takeaways**  
---  
  
  * AI issuance underwhelmed in September, in line with our expectations. However, this does not reflect weakening fundamentals or shortage of capital to fund the buildout. In our view, September's supply slowdown is due to a combination of 1) significant front-loading of issuance that happened in previous months, especially over the summer, 2) emerging signs of regulatory/political challenges to new data center construction, and 3) the rates sell-off possibly requiring project-level renegotiations for data-center deals. 
  * In US IG, we think the macro backdrop - and not elevated supply - is the biggest test between now and year-end, with outflows expected on the back of a sharp drawdown in returns. We expect at least one more deal in the US market, and note that HQ hyperscalers continue to tap non-USD currencies in between their larger US deals earlier this year. HQ hyperscalers should remain largely insensitive to higher rates, and we expect another wave of volatility into the fall, especially around 3Q26 earnings and likely further upward capex revisions. 
  * Lev Fin was active in September, but we expect 4Q26 to look more like 1Q/3Q, with a slower pace of deals given higher rates and regulatory/political limitations. Lower-quality issuers and project-level debt are more sensitive to the current rate environment, in our view, but issuers might be able to negotiate better lease economics with tenants to improve their returns. 
  * A handful of new securitized products deals came to market in September after a pause in August, bringing with them wider spreads and structural innovations. A floating-rate ABS deal and partial amortization in CMBS reflect the evolution the market is undergoing to attract incremental demand as the cost of debt for sponsors surges. We expect spreads to continue to leak wider from here, and reiterate our preference for colocation over hyperscaler data center ABS. Raising interest rate volatility could adversely affect the economics of data center securitization. 
  * For Single Name, despite lighter September issuance, off-cycle earnings and headline flow continue to drive elevated investor inbound. Both ORCL and NVDA, the latter a new addition to our coverage, remain central to these discussions, for their evolving funding strategies and their contribution to heightened lease documentation scrutiny. 

  
![](cid:image_dccc2f76-b125-11f1-b79c-85eb549cca22_1_4)  
---  
  
With ~$466bn of issuance YTD, we think 4Q supply might slow down sequentially,
while remaining above September's issuance pace. Different from last year,
when most of the supply came in 4Q, we expect a more moderate pace of issuance
in 4Q26, with different dynamics in each market: we expect hyperscalers to
come back to the US IG market and continue to tap non-USD currencies; supply
of data center paper in both the IG and HY markets is hard to predict as there
is certainly urgency to get construction going, but there is also more
sensitivity to higher rates. We also lowered our 2026 issuance estimates for
ABS/CMBS to $25-30bn, which implies another ~$5-10bn of supply in the upcoming
quarter.

Collateral-backed paper still has better risk-reward than unsecured
corporates, in our view.Within the universe of collateralized assets (~30% of
AI-related debt), construction risk on data center paper in the IG/HY markets
has been a significant driver of spread volatility on the back of headlines
about permit and power delays, as well as the risk of lease reassignment and
contract uncertainties ([ORCL's Force Majeure
episode](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/d8adcfc8-b858-11f1-a440-99a719172027?t=1790953505:9363:2233496:816774ccf5ea&m=1&ch=Outlook
Blastmail#e=ZmVsaXBlLm1vbnRlaXJvQGNhcHN0b25lLmNvbS5icg==)). Stabilized assets
in ABS/CMBS are therefore more insulated from such negative volatility. As for
chip financing, we think the nature of the assets allows for faster cash flow
generation and amortization, but there is still only a handful of public deals
that would allow investors to express this preference.

Despite better performance last month from the hyperscalers, we expect near-
term volatility amid rising rates/outflows going into the midterm elections
and likely another leg of upward capex revision at 3Q26 earnings. Looking past
4Q26, however, we think much of the hyperscaler decompression trade may have
played out: issuance cadence is becoming more (although not completely)
predictable, capex is shifting to shorter-dated assets (like chips), and
continued evidence of strong returns on AI capex underscore that the
fundamental story behind the spending remains robust.

| **2026 YTD issuance is now at $466bn, vs. $216bn in FY25 issuance**![](cid:image_dccc2f76-b125-11f1-b79c-85eb549cca22_1_5)**Source: Bloomberg, Pitchbook | LCD, CreditFlow, TREPP, Morgan Stanley Research estimates. Note: YTD 2026 data includes deals priced until 9/30/26. For a more detailed version of this exhibit, refer to Exhibit 3. 4a2 Priv. Plac. includes only the AVGO chip financing deal. Figures are rounded to the nearest $bn; totals are calculated using unrounded figures and may differ slightly from the sum of displayed values.**  
---  
  


**~70% of AI-related debt is unsecured corporate
issuance**![](cid:image_dccc2f76-b125-11f1-b79c-85eb549cca22_1_6)**Source:
Bloomberg, Company filings, Morgan Stanley Research. For data center breakdown
and rel val, seeExhibit 9 and Exhibit 5.**  
---

TMT Credit Research  
ORCL Credit: Lighthouse in the Fog  
| | [Read Full Report](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/ebd72d32-b82c-11f1-a440-99a719172027?t=1790804754:2763:1648850:95722cac585c&m=1&ch=CDF Research ISG#e=ZmVsaXBlLm1vbnRlaXJvQGNhcHN0b25lLmNvbS5icg==)  
---  
(PDF: 6 Pages)  
---  
| North America  
---  
Lindsay A Tyler, Benjamin Guerrero  
September 30, 2026  
---  
The site in question: The Wisconsin "Lighthouse" project is one of two Vantage
sites under development to be leased by ORCL. Contracted in September 2025,
this campus is planned to comprise of four data center buildings totaling
~902MW critical IT load.What's new: An infrastructure analytics firm stated in
a release that there is a material risk that meaningful load is not available
until mid-2028 for this site. That contrasts with ORCL's June guidance for
initial delivery beginning in CY2H27 and its September call characterization
of the project as "very much on track and going well" (and [updates in a
blog](https://www.oracle.com/news/announcement/blog/a-responsible-path-
forward-for-project-lighthouse-2026-09-16/)), although the timing remains
broadly consistent with [Vantage's stated ](https://vantage-dc.com/data-
center-locations/north-america/port-washington-wisconsin)2028 full-campus
completion target. The third-party report brings renewed attention to an
already-public PSC process. We are responding given 1) the complexity of
tracking these large ORCL-tied sites and the broader investor focus now re-
emerging around them, and 2) additional thoughts to share on the ORCL credit
implications of hypothetical delays at Lighthouse in WI, Jupiter in NM, or
elsewhere._See our initial response regarding the Jupiter news last week:[TMT
Credit, Clean Tech Energy, Corporate/Securitized Credit Strategy: Project
Jupiter Drifts Off Orbit – The Gravity of Force Majeure (25 Sep
2026)](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/d8adcfc8-b858-11f1-a440-99a719172027?ch=rp&sch=ar)_Considerations
for ORCL credit for any hypothetical project delay: We would be careful to not
just view slower potential delivery, in the instance of any site, solely
through the lens of near-term capex relief. While a possible delay could push
associated GPU and infrastructure spending to the right, which could be
helpful from a technical supply lens, we share a few offsetting
considerations:

  1. Revenue and cash-flow realization would be deferred, extending the period before confirmation that ORCL's substantial investment and contracted backlog are translating well into meaningful financial results.
  2. Delays could make the eventual balance-sheet and cash-flow impact more lumpy. If multiple halls are construction-ready by the time power is secured, ORCL could face more concentration in GPU capex (i.e., cash needs) and lease liabilities (i.e., balance-sheet obligations).
  3. Just as there is limited visibility into the underlying lease and financing documents, there is also limited visibility into the contractual terms supporting ORCL's RPO. It remains unclear whether customers have specified compute delivery timelines or what remedies may apply for delays.
  4. We consider whether any execution-risk overhang may spread to customer behavior and in turn pressure prepayments, [an important potential future funding source for ORCL](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/7a702140-ad63-11f1-8ecd-723b2bfc0461?ch=rp&sch=ar#/exhibit=1), either by affecting new RPO signings or customers' willingness to re-contract.

Power access again the key issue here, not construction: Similar to Project
Jupiter, shell construction appears to be progressing for Lighthouse (Exhibit
1), but timing increasingly hinges on power availability. ORCL (or a
subsidiary) appears to be the direct contracted party for power at both sites,
though the solutions differ with Jupiter relying on on-site generation.
Lighthouse requires Wisconsin PSC approval of ATC transmission infrastructure
to serve the campus from the grid via We Energies, subsidiary of WEC. The PSC
had been reviewing ATC's application, but ultimately [revoked its completeness
determination](https://psc.wi.gov/Pages/CommissionActions/CasePages/OzaukeeTransmission.aspx),
prompting a [recent refiling on a new
docket](https://psc.wi.gov/Pages/CommissionActions/CasePages/OzaukeeDIP.aspx).
(Separately, WEC has noted that [ORCL’s S&P
downgrade](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/c5b8c4b0-7bca-11f1-afb7-ebdda49ca146?ch=rp&sch=ar)
triggered additional collateral, with the current rating already requiring
full credit support.)| Within its June FY4Q26 earnings deck, ORCL provided
images of specific sites, including this one, to demonstrate "massive
progress" ![](cid:image_ebd72d32-b82c-11f1-a440-99a719172027_1_4) Source: ORCL
FY26 [earnings presentation
](https://investor.oracle.com/financials/default.aspx)(screenshot of slide 14)  
---  
  
Refresher on Stargate sites, construction loans and considerations: Lighthouse
and Shackelford are being funded through the ~$38bn financing first reported
in September 2025, part of ~$65bn of shorter-dated loans for ORCL-tied sites
outside the better-known $14bn RDMICH bond (Exhibit 2). As with Jupiter,
limited visibility into the financing and lease documents makes it difficult
to assess how delay consequences, if any, would be allocated among developers,
ORCL, lenders, and other counterparties. We continue to consider whether
greater focus on project delays could spill into ORCL CDS hedging, and whether
execution concerns – alongside higher rates and a growing DC construction debt
pool – could complicate the eventual refinancing of Abilene debt into longer-
dated paper as the project nears completion (6 of 8 buildings delivered).

There have been ~$65bn of short-dated construction loans and a separate ~$14bn
IG bond raised to fund Stargate-related shells, spanning an estimated ~5GW
critical IT for ORCL to lease amidst its broader 10GW+ build
![](cid:image_ebd72d32-b82c-11f1-a440-99a719172027_1_5) Source: Company
filings, Bloomberg (see article dated 4/24/26 for $38bn and $18bn mentions,
among other articles dating back in Sept '25), Morgan Stanley Research

![](https://vitalknowledge.net/assets/images/resources//section1.png)  
---  
| | ![](https://vitalknowledge.net/assets/images/resources//vertical_divider.png) INTRADAY COMMENTARY   
---  
Oct 07, 2026 5:08:07 PM EST  
AI update: WSJ report on AI financing underscores why yields can't go down,
plus a look at APLD earnings  
  
  * **AI’s debt bonanza continues –** the WSJ published [an article](https://www.wsj.com/tech/oracle-broadcom-and-spacex-seek-blockbuster-debt-deals-to-pay-for-ai-chips-848e8032?mod=newsviewer_click&adobe_mc=MCMID%3D14817580030074134273340885069550229474%7CMCORGID%3DCB68E4BA55144CAA0A4C98A5%2540AdobeOrg%7CTS%3D1791407188) around 5pmET Wed night discussing a **series of mega financing deals being worked on in the AI industry** , including for **OpenAI/Broadcom** (~$50B to fund OpenAI’s custom chip, which is being developed with Broadcom), **Oracle** (which is talking to Apollo and Goldman about raising cash for chip purchases), and **SpaceX/Nvidia** (SpaceX is in talks to raise ~$40B for Nvidia chip purchases – this was first reported by the FT Tues night). No one will be surprised by any of the WSJ details, but the **article makes clear that the tidal wave of AI-linked debt is still building, and until the momentum cools, it will be very hard for Treasury yields to go down**.
  * **APLD (Applied Digital)** reported a **huge beat in FQ1 on revenue** (+322% Y/Y to $342MM vs. the Street $124MM) and **adjusted EBITDA**($64.4MM vs. the Street $43.1MM), although **the “purchase of property and equipment” number (aka capex) was massive** (which was $2.074B, up ~730% Y/Y), and **far outpaced op. cash flow** (which was $64MM) while **stock-based comp was nearly equal to adjusted EBITDA** (SBC came in at $59.4MM, up 311% Y/Y), and the **lease backlog numbers didn’t change in FQ1 vs. FQ4** (total leases represent ~$36B of contracted revenue over their initial base terms, or approximately $86B if all renewal options are exercises – these numbers are the same as in the FQ4 press release). **Bottom Line** : these results exemplify the extremes of the AI industry, w/rapid top line growth but huge capital requirements.

_Market commentary, not research._



AI jitters subside (for now). Earnings can get markets on track – or break
them.



**Earnings are saying “risk-on”; bonds are saying “beware”.** For now,
earnings are winning. But if the US 10-year keeps rising and credit spreads
begin to widen, the author appears to believe that is when the equity/AI
narrative becomes materially more vulnerable.



**_If you're looking for a compelling weekend read, Chris Wood has just
released the latest 119-page edition of Asia Maxima, titled “[Reverberating
Tremors](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14171498&ad=4982845182&h=Qze1M_Q&sig=a42z0U4J8YofYGUeRDLBVOE0Rll&v=2&url=https://javatar.bluematrix.com/links2/secure/pdf/7a99ab23-0dab-43db-a155-a457b6ca3f16)”.
_**



Chris is essentially making the same argument:



**Higher nominal growth + fiscal stress → higher long-end yields → higher cost
of capital → more expensive AI debt financing → pressure on hyperscaler
returns → wider credit spreads → eventual break in AI capex/equities.**



So the tension is quite powerful: **earnings are saying “risk-on”; bonds are
saying “beware”.** For now, earnings are winning. But if the US 10-year keeps
rising and credit spreads begin to widen, Chris believes that is **when the
equity/AI narrative becomes materially more vulnerable.**

** **

I’m with Chris—hard not to be. The winning portfolio still looks refreshingly
old-school: gold, energy, banks, semiconductor scarcity, hard assets, and
businesses generating visible, dependable cash flows.**_ _**

---  
| | Investors increasingly focused last quarter on a dramatic sell-off in G7 government bond markets, a renewed Federal Reserve tightening cycle and a renewed break out of hostilities in the Middle East. But for now at least equities remain supported by stellar earnings growth courtesy primarily of the still accelerating AI capex cycle.  
---  
| | The sell-off in long term government bonds reflects the surge in nominal GDP growth, most particularly in America and Japan, as well as rising fiscal concerns. This has confirmed again that G7 government bonds are in a structural bear market while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s failed efforts to suppress yields last quarter has renewed expectations of Japanese-like policies of financial repression in the US, be it so-called Treasury QE or yield curve control.The ten-year Treasury bond yield remains the most important price in world financial markets. But the arrival of a new Fed chair has increased the importance of the American central bank given Kevin Warsh’s stated commitment at the September FOMC meeting to hit the 2% inflation target when inflation has now been above that target in the US for more than five years.The key issue for US equities remains whether the hyperscalers will be able to make a return on their massive AI-related investments. As these investments are increasingly funded by debt rather than cash, the cycle is most likely to end when markets are no longer willing to fund these investments. This risk grows the more interest rates rise. For this reason credit spreads should be monitored closely. The long-term base case, or end game, remains massive capital destruction in the US.As regards geopolitics financial markets have, for the most part, remained remarkably calm amidst continuing dramatic newsflow, be it concerning the Middle East or the Russian-Ukraine conflict which intensified last quarter. Most importantly, the conflict with Iran remains far from resolved.China continues to post a record trade surplus reflecting its dominance in global manufacturing and a related ongoing boom in intra-emerging market trade. Still there remains a lack of consumption boosting measures even though Beijing is formally committed to boosting the role of consumption. Indeed household borrowing is now declining in outright terms.Gold has continued to consolidate after last year’s historic rally. Still the world has moved to a _de facto_ gold standard as central banks continue to own more gold than US treasury bonds. The base case is that the dollar debasement trade is only in temporary abeyance though the actions of the Warsh Fed should be monitored closely.| **US 10-year Treasury bond yield**

Finance Wave  
| | [Read Full Report](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/14b70596-c300-11f1-9a76-0c9193771472?t=1791465037:2951:9323:5e2e4f67363b&m=1&ch=CDF Research ISG#e=ZmVsaXBlLm1vbnRlaXJvQGNhcHN0b25lLmNvbS5icg==)  
---  
(PDF: 7 Pages)  
---  
| North America  
---  
Lindsay A Tyler, Nishant Satyam, Benjamin Guerrero  
October 8, 2026  
---  
The WSJ reports that ORCL may be entering the creative chip-financing mix
through a structure in which a third-party entity purchases chips and leases
them back to ORCL, as soon as this year, though did not provide sizing (we are
not aware of a company response nor of a deal). That closely matches the chip-
lease SPV framework we have long hypothesized, even going back to our December
2025 earnings reaction.| One key chip financing structure – which we refer to
as a chip-lease SPV – uses an intermediary SPV that purchases chips from a
supplier and leases them to an AI customer, and the debt raise is backed by
the lease and amortizing.
![](cid:image_14b70596-c300-11f1-9a76-0c9193771472_1_4) Source: Morgan Stanley
Research. Note: Presented in our December earnings response. Also see our June
deck for more on such structures (note select trades stale): [GPUs, TPUs, &
IOUs: Insights on Contract- and Chip-Backed Debt Financings from the Corporate
Lens (3 Jun
2026)](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/315eb57e-5db9-11f1-bb82-5734c7383398?ch=rp&sch=ar).  
---  
  
As a reminder at a high-level, corporate motivations for potential bespoke
creative chip financing have included deferring upfront capex requirements,
diversifying funding sources, and potentially lowering cost of capital. The
two key asset/contract-backed structures are contract-backed term loans and
chip-lease SPV debt, both in the form of short-dated amortizing paper.

For ORCL specifically, a chip-lease SPV has seemed logical given our views
that its IG rating could serve a purpose in obtaining financing off of a
hypothetical commitment (now for chips, not just shells), its USD IG index
debt footprint should not expand significantly more toward that of large
financial issuers, and natural debt paydown in the out years could be prudent
to incorporate into the complex.

Until recently, however, management appeared content to rely on potential
future customer prepayments as the extra tool in the funding toolkit. What may
have changed is not only cost of capital for parent bonds (now at 7.5% for
ORCL 10y), but also the growing likelihood of a broader wave of creative chip
financing – i.e., shorter dated, amortizing paper backed by a chip lease or
compute contract. Since our August [NVDA credit
initiation](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/29875000-9ce2-11f1-b5c5-f551449e1153?ch=rp&sch=cr),
we've had extensive investor discussions on this, a recurring theme being
uncertainty over the market's capacity to absorb the sheer scale of
forthcoming GPU/XPU financing needs, with potential scaling beyond bank
lending and private credit into public markets.

In this context, top of mind – given semiconductor management commentary and a
June TPU deal – are potential additional structures designed to help unrated
and high-yield issuers meet upfront capex needs, aided by some form of
residual-value support or high-quality offtake (or pricing floor support). But
it is also possible that IG corporates – for upfront capex or even in sale-
leaseback format – may see value in establishing an early position before
creative chip financing possibly evolves into a large, crowded asset class.

For ORCL, from a ratings and accounting perspective, we would view a chip-
lease SPV to be debt-like, with the lease recognized on-balance-sheet at
commencement and incorporated into adjusted leverage assessments at the parent
level. We are also watching how already limited lease disclosures could evolve
with any introduction of 5Y chip operating leases.

If the reported deal indeed plays out, we would appreciate management's
efforts to diversify funding sources – which may also demonstrate willingness
to explore other currencies for unsecured and even hybrids. It's possible such
a chip lease deal, paired with other options, could reduce the need for a CY1H
bond deal, or at least limit near-term equity issuance or a reliance on
prepays. But we suspect any bond-market reaction to this headline – which
appears to be a fair move wider to start – will end up being driven less by
ORCL-specific supply implications and more by investor indigestion around the
prospective scale of the broader chip-financing wave. For ORCL as an IG
'tenant', we wonder whether its growing stock of leases could drive
incremental CDS hedging activity. Conversely, any form of NVDA support in a
hypothetical announced deal – though not currently our base case – would be
constructive for ORCL.

more...](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/14b70596-c300-11f1-9a76-0c9193771472?t=1791465037:2951:9323:5e2e4f67363b&m=1&ch=CDF
Research ISG#e=ZmVsaXBlLm1vbnRlaXJvQGNhcHN0b25lLmNvbS5icg==)
